arXiv:2605.11374v1 [cs.LG] 12 May 2026

Test-Time Compute for Dense Retrieval: Agentic Program Generation with Frozen Embedding Models

Han Xiao Affiliation: Jina AI by Elastic Email: han.xiao@jina.ai
Abstract

Test-time compute is widely believed to benefit only large reasoning models. We show it also helps small embedding models. Most modern embedding checkpoints are distilled from large LLM backbones and inherit their representation space; a frozen embedding model should therefore benefit from extra inference compute without retraining. Using an agentic program-search loop, we explore 259 candidate inference programs over a frozen embedding API across ninety generations. The entire Pareto frontier collapses onto a single algebra: a softmax-weighted centroid of the local top-KK documents interpolated with the query. This parameter-free default lifts nDCG@10 statistically significantly across seven embedding-model families spanning a tenfold parameter range, with held-out full-BEIR validation confirming the lift on every model tested.

1 Introduction

Test-time compute has transformed reasoning in generative language models. Best-of-NN sampling (Brown et al., 2024), self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023b), and verifier-guided search (Snell et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025) let a smaller model spend more inference FLOPs to match a larger one along a smooth Pareto curve. The common reading is that this scaling regime is reserved for large reasoning LLMs and that small models have nothing to gain. Dense retrieval, dominated by small embedding models, has correspondingly not had its test-time-compute moment. Frozen embedding models such as jina-embeddings-v5-text-small (j-v5-small), e5-base-v2, and gte-base-en-v1.5 are deployed with one forward pass per query and one cosine similarity per document.

We argue that the small-model picture is misleading. Most modern embedding models are distilled or initialised from large LLM backbones. Qwen3-Embedding (Zhang et al., 2025) starts from the Qwen3 foundation models and inherits their representation space. EmbeddingGemma (Vera et al., 2025) is built on Gemma 3 and uses its long-context backbone. j-v5 (Akram et al., 2026) is distilled from Qwen3 with task-LoRA adapters on top. SFR-Embedding-2 (Meng et al., 2024) is fine-tuned from Mistral-7B. NV-Embed-v2 (Lee et al., 2025) adapts a decoder-only LLM with latent attention. GritLM (Muennighoff et al., 2025) unifies generative and embedding capabilities in a single Mistral-based model. To the extent that test-time compute is a property of the underlying LLM representation space, these distilled small embedding models should inherit at least some of that potential. Existing test-time scaling proposals for retrieval require an external generative LLM (Gao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023a), a second supervisory retriever (Uzan et al., 2026), or trained extra parameters (Xiao et al., 2026). This work asks a stricter question: how much can a frozen single-vector embedding model gain at inference, with no auxiliary model and no new parameters?

We answer with an agentic program-search loop in which an LLM proposer writes Python programs over the frozen embedding API, a harness scores each candidate on a multi-task retrieval benchmark, and a lesson ledger accumulates ruled-out hypotheses as long-horizon memory. Section 3 describes the loop architecture. Section 4 reports the emergent structure of the search output. Section 5 validates the discovered programs on held-out full-BEIR tasks across seven embedding-model families and connects the winning program to classical pseudo-relevance feedback.

2 Related Work

2.1 Test-time compute for generative LLMs

Best-of-NN scaling forms the dominant test-time compute paradigm for generative LLMs. Snell et al. (2025) formalize compute-optimal allocation between best-of-NN sampling and iterative revision. Brown et al. (2024) show best-of-NN scales coverage log-linearly. Wu et al. (2025) establish a clean inference scaling Pareto frontier on math problem-solving. Wang et al. (2023b) introduce majority-vote over sampled chains-of-thought. Common to all four is stochasticity: sample many noisy candidates, then aggregate. We adopt the same question—whether extra inference compute can substitute for a larger embedding model—and find the embedding analogue is structural rather than stochastic.

2.2 Generation-based query expansion

HyDE (Gao et al., 2023) embeds an LLM-generated hypothetical answer in place of the query; Query2Doc (Wang et al., 2023a) concatenates the LLM expansion to the query before encoding. Both rely on an external LLM at query time, trading inference latency and cost for retrieval gain. Zhuang et al. (2024) prompt LLMs to generate dense+sparse representations directly. We restrict ourselves to the embedding model itself, with no generative model in the inference path.

2.3 Pseudo-relevance feedback

Classical PRF (Rocchio, 1971; Robertson et al., 1995) re-formulates the query using terms from initial top-ranked documents. The de-facto sparse-PRF baseline is RM3 (Lavrenko and Croft, 2001), which interpolates the original query with a relevance language model estimated from pseudo-relevant documents and remains a strong baseline on top of BM25. Learned sparse retrievers such as SPLADE (Formal et al., 2021) likewise rely on lexical expansion.

Recent dense PRF work takes three distinct routes. CEQE (Naseri et al., 2021) operates at the term level via contextualized embeddings. VPRF (Li et al., 2023a) aggregates top-kk dense embeddings into a vector-PRF query update. ANCE-PRF (Yu et al., 2021) trains a small reranker to consume top-kk embeddings. VPRF is the closest training-free prior art, since it computes a uniform mean over the top-kk retrieved-document embeddings and interpolates with the query. Our work can be seen as extending VPRF by replacing the uniform mean with a softmax-temperature-weighted centroid and adding an interpolation coefficient α\alpha; Section 5 validates this across 13 tasks and seven embedding-model families.

A separate line of recent vector-PRF extensions brings an LLM into the inference loop, including LLM-VPRF (Li et al., 2025b), GPRF (Tu et al., 2026), and PromptPRF (Li et al., 2025a). These lie in a different inference regime than the training-free, no-LLM substrate explored here. PromptPRF reports that LLM-extracted features over PRF documents narrow the gap between small and large dense retrievers. We observe a similar small-model lift without requiring an LLM in the inference path.

The relationship between the programs discovered by our search and classical PRF is discussed in Section 6.

2.4 Test-time scaling for retrieval

MetaEmbed (Xiao et al., 2026) adds learnable Meta-Tokens that produce a flexible multi-vector representation, scaling accuracy with the number of tokens kept at test time. It requires training. GQR (Uzan et al., 2026) performs gradient descent on the query embedding using a second model’s similarity as supervision. It requires a secondary retriever. Both target multimodal hybrid retrieval. Late interaction in ColBERT and ColBERTv2 (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020; Santhanam et al., 2022) is another way to spend more compute per query, but at the cost of multi-vector storage. Our regime is strictly more constrained, requiring a frozen single-vector embedding model, no second model, and no extra forward pass for the cheapest variant.

2.5 Program generation and agentic discovery

Closest to our methodological framing are LLM-driven program-generation loops in which a language model proposes candidate programs, an evaluator scores them, and the surviving programs condition the next round of proposals. FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) discovered new constructions for the cap set problem and bin packing this way. AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) extended the pattern to a coding agent capable of improving algorithmic primitives. ELM (Lehman et al., 2024) explored LLM-assisted evolution earlier. Our agent loop is an instance of the same pattern, specialized to embedding-program search. The proposer is conditioned on a Pareto frontier over cost and Δ\DeltanDCG, plus a structured log of which substrate families the search has already moved beyond. The evaluator is a pinned multi-task retrieval harness. To our knowledge this is the first time this loop has been applied to the dense-retrieval inference recipe.

3 Methodology

The central contribution of this paper is a rerunnable agentic loop that discovers embedding programs for dense retrieval.11 1 Code, program registry, lesson ledger, and evaluation harness: https://github.com/hanxiao/embedding-ttc An LLM proposer explores a structured search space of embedding-level operations. A harness scores each candidate on a fixed multi-task retrieval benchmark under a GPU lock. A lesson ledger accumulates ruled-out hypotheses so the agent does not revisit structurally equivalent ideas. Section 4 reports what the loop produced across ninety generations of search, including the emergent algebraic structure of the Pareto frontier. Section 5 reports the cross-model validation at full-BEIR scale.

3.1 Outer loop

The agent runs as a cron-driven generation loop, with one full iteration laid out in Algorithm 1. At the start of each generation gg a proposer reads three inputs: the current Pareto frontier ℱg−1\mathcal{F}_{g-1} over cost and average Δ\DeltanDCG@10; the per-cell evaluation history over six universal cells, defined as two embedding-model sizes by three retained tasks {NFCorpus, SciFact, ArguAna}, with FiQA-2018 evaluated on every program as a separate stress task that does not gate frontier admission; and a structured log of meta-lessons accumulated from prior generations. The proposer then writes one or two new programs as Python functions and appends them to a versioned registry v{g}.py. A separate runner process acquires a GPU lock, evaluates each newly registered program on all six universal cells over a small hyperparameter sweep, writes results to a JSONL ledger, and logs the outcome as HIT, MARGINAL, MISS, or non-universal back into the meta-lesson record for the next generation.

3.2 Proposer

The proposer is an LLM agent that writes Python programs over the frozen embedding model API. It is bound by a four-rule contract. Each new program must touch a substrate family, a named category of embedding-space operations such as centroid replacement, LoRA fusion, or stochastic ensembling, that the lesson ledger does not mark closed. It must branch on argmax or argpartition or use only structurally fixed thresholds. It must cite at least one of six fixed proposal principles, such as “argmax over confidence, not over output values”. And it must justify why the program is not equivalent under composition to any program already in ℛ\mathcal{R}. The structural-threshold rule prevents the proposer from quietly tuning hyperparameters into the program text. The agent is otherwise unconstrained. It may manipulate text, introduce conditional gates, operate in score space, combine LoRA adapters, or compose operations in any order. The proposer is free to mutate hyperparameters of an existing program, recombine two parents, or open a new substrate family. Generation-by-generation behaviour is logged in PROGRAM_LOG.md.

3.3 Lesson ledger

The lesson ledger is the loop’s memory. Each generation appends which substrate families were ruled out, which compositions are redundant, and which families still have open hypotheses. Two representative entries from PROGRAM_LOG.md, surfaced verbatim in the registry conditioning prompt, illustrate the discipline. The first records that stochastic ensembling returns no signal on any of the six universal cells: the median of unit-norm embeddings leaves the unit sphere and there is no verifier to pick a winning sample, unlike LLM best-of-NN. The second records that raw-document HyDE with majority gates collapses by construction, because each top-kk document viewed as a pseudo-query retrieves itself with similarity one. The ledger keeps the proposer from revisiting structurally equivalent ideas under new names and is the principal reason the search remains productive across ninety generations.

3.4 Evaluation harness

Programs are evaluated on six universal cells, formed by crossing {j-v5-small, j-v5-nano} with {NFCorpus, SciFact, ArguAna}, plus FiQA-2018 as an additional stress cell on each embedding model. The four-task baseline reproductions in Appendix Table 8 cover the same eight cells. Each cell runs MTEB v2.8.4 with a fixed dataset revision. Per-query nDCG@10 is logged so that paired bootstrap significance can be computed post hoc against any baseline. A program is called universal if all six universal cells are non-negative. Otherwise it is recorded but does not enter the frontier.

The cost axis used to admit programs to the frontier is the per-query encoder forward-pass count. Per-query test-time complexity in dense retrieval decomposes into three components. Let FF denote the encoder forward-pass cost, NN the corpus size, dd the embedding dimension, NcN_{c} the first-stage candidate pool depth, and KK the local centroid radius. The trivial program P0P_{0} runs in 𝒪⁡(F+d​N)\mathcal{O}(F+dN) time for query encoding and dense scoring, or in 𝒪⁡(F+d​log⁡N)\mathcal{O}(F+d\log N) when an ANN index replaces the dense scan. A frontier program at c×c\times encoder cost runs in 𝒪⁡(c​F+d​Nc+d​K)\mathcal{O}(cF+dN_{c}+dK). This decomposes into cc encoder forward passes for the query and any re-encoded anchors, one 𝒪⁡(d​Nc)\mathcal{O}(dN_{c}) matrix-vector multiply over the candidate pool to score against the updated query, and an 𝒪⁡(d​K)\mathcal{O}(dK) aggregation to compute the centroid. The 𝒪⁡(c​F)\mathcal{O}(cF) term dominates because FF is roughly 10 to 50 ms per query for transformer encoders, while d​NcdN_{c} is about 0.050.05 ms at Nc=1000N_{c}{=}1000 and d=1024d{=}1024 on a single CPU thread. The cost factor cc is therefore the meaningful test-time scaling axis. The agent’s frontier is admitted by the pair cc and Δ​nDCG​@​10\Delta\mathrm{nDCG@10}, with cc counted in encoder forward passes.

We track three frontier strata. The 1×1\times stratum requires no extra encoder pass and only matrix-vector arithmetic over precomputed embeddings. The 2×2\times stratum allows one extra encoder pass for an anchor re-encoding. The ≥4×\geq 4\times stratum allows multiple anchors or LoRA re-encodings. Within 1×1\times all costs are dominated by the 𝒪⁡(d​Nc)\mathcal{O}(dN_{c}) matrix-vector multiply, which we treat as effectively free. Appendix B reports the empirical scaling of Δ\Delta nDCG@10 against cc across the registry of 1,522 evaluations. We use “encoder cost” and “encoder forward pass” as standard technical terms throughout, both referring to one forward pass of the embedding model.

Section 4.2 reports the runtime trajectory of the loop, including the cumulative discovery curve and the substrate-family breakdown of programs proposed and ruled out.

4 Agentic Discovered Programs

The proposer agent is not constrained to a predefined grammar. Each program is an arbitrary Python function over a minimal interface: a frozen embedding model fθf_{\theta} mapping text to unit-norm vectors, a precomputed document index DD with embeddings 𝐝i=fθ​(di)\mathbf{d}_{i}=f_{\theta}(d_{i}), and retrieval via si=fθ​(q)⊤​𝐝is_{i}=f_{\theta}(q)^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{i}. The agent is free to manipulate text through sentence splitting, truncation, and instruction prefixes. It may introduce conditional branching through gap-confidence gates, robustness witnesses, and overlap checks. It may operate in score space using Borda, RRF, or z-score fusion. It may combine multiple LoRA adapters. It may compose these operations in any order. This open-ended freedom is what makes the centroid-algebra finding non-trivial. The rest of this section reports the structure the agent independently re-derived as the simplest hypothesis consistent with the universal-positive criterion across all rounds of search.

4.1 Emergent algebraic structure

Every program on the discovered Pareto frontier is a structured update that moves the query toward a local document centroid, followed by re-ranking with the updated query. Programs in structurally different families, such as stochastic ensembles, score-space fusion, cascade reranking, asymmetric LoRA encoding, and text perturbation, were explored across ninety rounds of search, and the frontier concentrated exclusively on centroid-algebra programs, sharpening the structural claim by exhausting alternative substrate families.

Post hoc, every frontier program reduces to a composition of five operations:

enc(text,adapter,prefix)→ℝdretr(𝐯,D,k)→𝒯k⊆{1,…,N}aggr({𝐝i}i∈𝒯k;op)→ℝdintp(𝐯1,𝐯2,α)→ℝdrerank(D′;𝐪′)→ranked list\begin{aligned} \textsc{enc}&(\textit{text};\,\textit{adapter},\,\textit{prefix})\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\\ \textsc{retr}&(\mathbf{v};\,D,\,k)\to\mathcal{T}_{k}\subseteq\{1,\dots,N\}\\ \textsc{aggr}&(\{\mathbf{d}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{k}};\,\textit{op})\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\\ \textsc{intp}&(\mathbf{v}_{1},\,\mathbf{v}_{2};\,\alpha)\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\\ \textsc{rerank}&(D^{\prime};\,\mathbf{q}^{\prime})\to\text{ranked list}\end{aligned}

with aggr parameterized by op∈{mean,softmaxτ,max}\textit{op}\in\{\text{mean},\text{softmax}_{\tau},\text{max}\}. This is not a search space we defined upfront. It is a finding. The agent explored seventeen substrate families spanning text manipulation, gating, score-space arithmetic, multi-LoRA routing, and stochastic sampling, as Section 4.2 documents. The entire Pareto frontier collapsed into this simple algebra. The baseline is the trivial program P0=rerank​(D,enc​(q))P_{0}=\textsc{rerank}(D;\textsc{enc}(q)). Every frontier program extends it by inserting a retrieve-aggregate-interpolate step between encoding and reranking.

The emergent structure varies along three axes. An aggregation axis selects between mean and softmax-weighted, with or without a similarity floor. An anchor axis selects among top-kk document embeddings, a first-sentence pseudo-document, and title-only encoding. A gate axis selects among always-fire, gap-confidence, and robustness-witness conditions. All three axes share the same geometric template: move the query toward a local centroid, then rerank. Representative frontier programs are schematized as flow diagrams in Appendix G.

Three concrete programs ground the empirical sections. The first is embedding-space Rocchio: given the initial query embedding 𝐪=fθ​(q)\mathbf{q}=f_{\theta}(q) and the indices of the top-KK retrieved documents 𝒯K\mathcal{T}_{K}, the updated query is

𝐪′=normalize(𝐪+β⋅1K∑i∈𝒯K𝐝i).\mathbf{q}^{\prime}=\mathrm{normalize}\!\left(\mathbf{q}+\beta\cdot\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{K}}\mathbf{d}_{i}\right). (1)

We call this Rocchio. The only new compute is one ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} argpartition over NN scores, one mean over KK vectors, and one extra ℝd×ℝd×N\mathbb{R}^{d}{\times}\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} matrix product. Because 𝐝i\mathbf{d}_{i} is precomputed, no additional encoder forward pass is needed. We call this 1×1\times encoder cost.

The second program, SoftCentroid, replaces the simple mean with a temperature-controlled softmax over initial similarities and interpolates the query toward the resulting centroid:

wi\displaystyle w_{i} =exp⁡(𝐪⊤​𝐝i/τ)∑j∈𝒯Kexp⁡(𝐪⊤​𝐝j/τ),\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{i}/\tau)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{K}}\exp(\mathbf{q}^{\top}\mathbf{d}_{j}/\tau)}, (2)
𝐪′\displaystyle\mathbf{q}^{\prime} =normalize⁡((1−α)​𝐪+α​∑i∈𝒯Kwi​𝐝i).\displaystyle=\mathrm{normalize}\!\left((1-\alpha)\mathbf{q}+\alpha\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}_{K}}w_{i}\mathbf{d}_{i}\right). (3)

At α=1\alpha{=}1 the query is fully replaced by the centroid; at τ→0\tau\to 0 the centroid collapses to the top-1 document. With α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, τ=0.05\tau{=}0.05, and K∈{2,3}K\in\{2,3\}, SoftCentroid is the strongest 1×1\times program found.

The third program, FirstSent, takes the top-1 retrieved document d(1)d^{(1)}, truncates it to its first sentence s(1)s^{(1)}, re-encodes that sentence, and interpolates the query toward the single anchor:

𝐪′=normalize⁡((1−α)​𝐪+α⋅fθ​(s(1))).\mathbf{q}^{\prime}=\mathrm{normalize}\!\left((1-\alpha)\mathbf{q}+\alpha\cdot f_{\theta}(s^{(1)})\right).

This costs one additional encoder forward pass per query at 2×2\times encoder cost. The per-corpus first-sentence cache amortizes across queries. The first sentence is extracted from the raw document body via the standard NLTK Punkt sentence tokenizer, not from a preprocessed title or abstract field. On corpora without natural sentence boundaries, such as code and dialogue, this anchor would need to be redefined.

The full set of substrate families the meta-program explored is enumerated in the supplementary alongside the relevant entries from the program log. The list includes LoRAFusion, DocChunk, QueryTemplate, DropoutEns, AsymLoRA, QueryRepeat, score-space Borda and RRF, per-LoRA z-score fusion, cascade reranking, and robustness gates.

4.2 Search trajectory

We first examine the program-search trajectory to understand how programs evolve and what compute-accuracy tradeoffs emerge.

The loop ran for ninety generations across roughly three wall-clock days, registering 259 programs across seventeen substrate families and evaluating 10,535 configurations. The proposer used Claude Opus 4 with a long-horizon prompt that includes the current Pareto frontier and lesson ledger. One generation cost approximately 0.300.30 in API charges and produced one or two new programs. Total proposer cost was approximately $30\$30 over the search. The cumulative discovery curve in Figure 3 flattens after generation 30 and saturates after generation 78, suggesting the 2×2\times universal frontier has been exhausted under the current encoder API. The trajectory reveals three distinct phases.

The search began with the substrates most directly inspired by LLM test-time compute. Cross-task LoRA fusion, dropout-based embedding ensembles, asymmetric LoRA encoding, and multi-prompt query templates are the natural analogues of best-of-NN sampling, self-consistency, and prompt engineering. All four were ruled out within the first ten rounds. The lesson ledger recorded the structural reason in each case. Stochastic ensembling has no verifier to select among samples, so its mean leaves the unit sphere into a metric the model was not trained to respect. Asymmetric LoRA encoding projects queries and documents into misaligned subspaces, which removes the geometric alignment the embedding model relies on. The agent therefore moved on quickly to substrates more aligned with the cosine geometry.

The first successful programs emerged from embedding-space Rocchio, a classical technique the agent independently re-derived. The proposer then began systematic variation with similarity floors, multi-round iteration, z-score normalization, and negative feedback. It discovered that replacing the uniform mean with a softmax-temperature-weighted centroid and adding an interpolation coefficient α\alpha produced a strictly better default. The SoftCentroid family crystallized around generation 25 with K=3,α=0.5,τ=0.05K{=}3,\alpha{=}0.5,\tau{=}0.05.

In the middle phase, the agent explored alternative anchors including first-sentence re-encoding, title-only encoding, document chunking, corpus-mean subtraction, and pseudo-document replacement. FirstSent became the 2×2\times frontier holder on ArguAna with gains of +6.9+6.9 to +7.3+7.3 nDCG@10. Score-space fusion methods and cascade reranking were explored and shown to be dominated by the centroid family. Once the centroid family was established, the agent turned to the question of when to apply programs, through gap-confidence gates, top-KK overlap witnesses, and robustness witnesses. These gates modestly improved worst-case behaviour but did not move the universal frontier.

The final twelve rounds covered instruction-prefix queries, document-side projection, title-as-anchor, and composite witnesses. They confirmed the saturation of the frontier identified earlier rather than extending it. The lesson ledger had accumulated 23 meta-lessons by this point, and the proposer’s novel-substrate rate dropped to zero, signalling a clean stopping point for the search.

A reader who only takes the winning program away from this paper will under-use the result. The frontier program is one realization of a search whose value lies in being rerunnable. Drop in a different embedding-model family, benchmark, or encoder API, and the same loop will produce a different frontier. The closest existing patterns are FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) and AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025). What is new here is the application surface, training-free dense retrieval, and the lesson-ledger discipline that drives the search toward structurally cleaner programs rather than novelty for its own sake.

4.3 Branching structure

The 259 programs form a directed acyclic graph of parent-child relationships, with each program citing its parents and the mutation or recombination that produced it. The seventeen substrate families cluster into three super-families. The centroid super-family covers Rocchio, SoftCentroid, FirstSent, Rocchio-floor, pseudo-document replacement, and title-anchor variants. It accounts for over 180 frontier-eligible programs whose common structure is a query update toward a local document centroid or anchor, varying in aggregation, anchor source, and gating. The stochastic super-family covers DropoutEns, AsymLoRA, QueryTemplate, QueryRepeat, and multi-prompt ensembling. Its 40 or so programs sit uniformly at or below baseline because no verifier exists to select among noisy embedding samples. The score-space super-family covers Borda, RRF, z-score fusion, cascade reranking, and per-LoRA fusion. Its 30 or so programs are occasionally marginal but never universal, because operating in score space rather than embedding space loses the geometric structure that makes centroid updates effective. Representative frontier programs are schematized as flow diagrams in Appendix G.

Of the 240 programs evaluated on the full set of six universal cells, 88 satisfy the strict universal-positive criterion of Δ≥0\Delta\geq 0 on all six cells. A further 55 programs are positive on five of six cells, with mean Δ\Delta from +2.3+2.3 to +2.7+2.7 nDCG@10. The near-universal cohort overlaps the universal-positive cohort in mean lift, suggesting that strict universality is a conservative admission criterion rather than a tight performance ceiling. The search produces a wide cohort of strong candidates above the trivial program P0P_{0}, and the universal default we report is a conservative pick from this cohort.

5 Experimental Results

With the search trajectory and emergent algebra established, we now validate whether the discovered programs generalize across tasks, embedding-model families, and corpus scales.

5.1 Experimental setup

The headline embedding models are j-v5-small and j-v5-nano (Akram et al., 2026), two recent task-LoRA models distilled from Qwen3 that ship four task-specialized adapters over a shared backbone, one each for retrieval, classification, clustering, and text-matching. This adapter design lets us also test cross-task LoRA fusion as a candidate substrate. Models use published HuggingFace weights in fp16. Evaluation uses MTEB v2.8.4 with the official task revisions (Muennighoff et al., 2023; Enevoldsen et al., 2025), and instruction prefixes follow the model card. The four headline retrieval tasks are NFCorpus (Boteva et al., 2016), SciFact (Wadden et al., 2020), ArguAna (Wachsmuth et al., 2018), and FiQA-2018 (Maia et al., 2018), which together span medical IR, scientific fact verification, counter-argument retrieval, and short-question to long-document financial QA, drawn from the BEIR collection (Thakur et al., 2021). Baselines reproduce published nDCG@10 within 0.4 nDCG points on all eight model-by-task cells (Appendix Table 8).

All reported numbers use a two-stage pipeline. A first-stage ANN retriever returns a top-NcN_{c} candidate pool that the embedding program rescores against 𝐪′\mathbf{q}^{\prime}. The discovered programs are insensitive to pool depth. Holding the default fixed and varying Nc∈{100,…,5000}N_{c}\in\{100,\dots,5000\}, SoftCentroid reproduces the same Δ\Delta nDCG@10 on all representative cells, because the centroid is built only from the local top-KK. The rescoring cost is one d×Ncd{\times}N_{c} matrix-vector multiply, around 0.050.05 ms at Nc=1000N_{c}{=}1000 and d=1024d{=}1024 on a single CPU thread, negligible against the 10 to 50 ms encoder forward pass.

Table 1 reports the oracle-best program per cell. To verify this is not overfitting, we run 5-fold random dev/test splits with a 50/50 ratio. The dev-selected SoftCentroid configuration retains 80% of oracle gain on j-v5-small NFCorpus, 67% on j-v5-nano NFCorpus, and 99% and 98% on the two ArguAna cells. On SciFact and FiQA, where oracle gains are below 0.7, dev-selected gains do not survive validation. We therefore restrict claims to NFCorpus and ArguAna.

5.2 Frontier programs on j-v5

We begin with the headline question: how large are the gains from the discovered programs on the embedding-model family used to drive the search?

PRF and centroid replacement dominate on NFCorpus, SciFact, and ArguAna across both models. Table 1 reports the best per-cell program. Symmetric retrieval admits the largest gains. On ArguAna, the smaller j-v5-nano embedding model running a length-3 FirstSent program outperforms the 2.8×2.8\times-larger j-v5-small embedding model’s single-forward baseline. The same program also lifts j-v5-small. The effect is program-level test-time compute substituting for embedding-model size on tasks whose query and document distributions coincide.

The recommended default fixes K=3K{=}3 as the grid median, α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 as the Rocchio midpoint, and τ=0.05\tau{=}0.05 as the lowest stable temperature. Paired-bootstrap resampling on per-query nDCG@10 with 10,00010{,}000 resamples avoids post-hoc selection bias. The default lifts NFCorpus by +2.37+2.37 on j-v5-small and +1.99+1.99 on j-v5-nano, ArguAna by +2.80+2.80 and +3.19+3.19, all at p<0.001p<0.001. SciFact and FiQA gains are within noise. The default never hurts by more than 0.6 nDCG@10 on any of the four tasks.

The frozen default also generalizes beyond the headline tasks. Applied unmodified across all 13 nanoBEIR retrieval tasks (Zeta Alpha, 2024) on both models, the median lift is +0.17+0.17 on j-v5-small and +0.27+0.27 on j-v5-nano, with both means positive, as Table 2 reports. The four headline tasks participated in the agentic loop’s frontier-admission gate. The other nine tasks are strictly held out from the search and serve as a zero-shot transfer probe. NanoBEIR uses a 50-query random sub-sample of each BEIR task, so paired-bootstrap pp-values are noisy at this sample size. HotpotQA on j-v5-small is the only cell that crosses p<0.05p<0.05 in the negative direction. j-v5-nano shows no significant regression across the full 13-task suite. Negative deltas concentrated on NQ, ArguAna, and SciFact at p∈[0.07,0.12]p\in[0.07,0.12] are consistent with sub-sample variance rather than a true performance deficit. The same ArguAna cell yields +3.19+3.19 at p<0.001p<0.001 on the full 1,406-query corpus in Table 1.

FiQA-2018 is the short-finance-question to long-financial-document cell, where the global K=3K{=}3 default lands closest to baseline on the nanoBEIR slice. A targeted re-sweep along KK alone produced larger gains on the 50-query nano slice but those slice-sized gains do not replicate at full-BEIR scale on the same embedding models. Paired-bootstrap stat-sig on per-query nDCG@10 reveals that the K=10K{=}10 SoftCentroid variant is statistically significantly negative on full-BEIR FiQA for both j-v5-small at p=.022p{=}.022 and j-v5-nano at p=.0002p{=}.0002, reinforcing the model-specificity finding that K=10K{=}10 belongs to monolithic embedding models rather than the multi-LoRA j-v5 family.

Two negative ledger entries from the same nano sweep sharpen the picture. A five-prefix max-pool ensemble lands below baseline on both models, since the retrieval-LoRA already absorbs query-intent prefixing. A 1.5×1.5\times-cost last-paragraph PRF program is asymmetric across model sizes, lifting j-v5-nano but hurting j-v5-small.

5.3 Parameter sensitivity and compute regimes

A one-parameter ablation around the SoftCentroid default reveals that interpolation α\alpha and softmax temperature τ\tau carry most of the gain. Low τ\tau adds +2.5+2.5 to +2.9+2.9 on ArguAna, and moving from α=0.2\alpha{=}0.2 to α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 adds +0.6+0.6 to +1.8+1.8. Centroid size KK is largely inert, with ≤0.5\leq 0.5 across K∈{3,5,8}K\in\{3,5,8\}. Appendix D reports the full grid. Two compute regimes account for all meaningful gains. In the 1×1\times regime, extscSoftCentroid uses no extra encoder forward pass: all operations are matrix-vector arithmetic over precomputed embeddings, adding sub-millisecond overhead per query. This regime delivers all NFCorpus and SciFact gains and most of ArguAna. In the 2×2\times regime, extscFirstSent re-encodes the first sentence of the top-retrieved document, incurring one additional encoder forward pass per query. This regime buys an additional +0.6+0.6 to +0.8+0.8 nDCG@10 on ArguAna only. Above 2×2\times nothing moves the universal frontier. Figure 6 and Table 9 show that the cost-accuracy curve is concave and flattens hard above 2×2\times, in contrast to the log-linear best-of-NN scaling reported for generative LLMs (Brown et al., 2024). The best mean Δ\Delta nDCG@10 is +2.62+2.62 at 2×2\times, +2.67+2.67 at 33 to 4×4\times, and +2.65+2.65 above 4×4\times across the agent’s full registry of 1,522 program-task evaluations.

5.4 Cross-model transfer

A natural follow-up is whether programs discovered on one embedding-model family transfer to architecturally distinct models at different parameter scales.

The default SoftCentroid transfers to five monolithic embedding-model families at full-BEIR scale: the e5 family at three sizes e5-small-v2, e5-base-v2, and e5-large-v2 (Wang et al., 2022); gte-base-en-v1.5 (Li et al., 2023b); and bge-large-en-v1.5, evaluated on the four retrieval headlines plus NQ where data permits. The default lifts ArguAna by ten nDCG@10 points on e5-base-v2 and by three points on gte-base-en-v1.5, both at p<0.0001p<0.0001. NFCorpus lifts by over one point on both models at p<0.001p<0.001. Both models reach two of four cells at p<0.05p<0.05 on full BEIR. SciFact and FiQA-2018 are weaker, as Table 3 records. Combined with the j-v5 full-BEIR rows in Table 1, NFCorpus and ArguAna lift positively under default SoftCentroid on all seven embedding-model families tested at full-BEIR scale.

The optimal cluster size KK varies along a clean structural line. The multi-LoRA j-v5 family prefers K=3K{=}3 on the 13-task nanoBEIR suite, while both monolithic embedding models we test prefer K=10K{=}10. At the 13-task scale, the K=10K{=}10 variant produces positive deltas on 1010 of 1313 nanoBEIR retrieval cells on e5-base-v2, with the largest gains on MS MARCO and ClimateFEVER, as recorded in Appendix F. One reading is that the retrieval LoRA on j-v5 produces sharper local clusters where K=3K{=}3 already covers the relevant centroid mass, while monolithic BERT-base embedding models with instruction prefixes produce more diffuse clusters that benefit from a wider KK. The algebra and the qualitative finding transfer across all seven embedding-model families.

A parameter-scale ladder on the e5 family at full-BEIR shows the algebra is robust across model sizes within a family, as Table 3 reports. The headline ArguAna lift is approximately stable at eight to ten nDCG@10 points across a tenfold parameter range from e5-small-v2 at 33M to e5-large-v2 at 335M. bge-large-en-v1.5 confirms the algebra also works on a larger member of the BGE family. The earlier weakness on bge-base-en-v1.5 is therefore a model-specific gap rather than a parameter-scale lower bound. e5-small-v2 at the same 33M parameter count as bge-small-en-v1.5 is fully positive on three of four cells, while bge-small-en-v1.5 is the boundary case where only K=10K{=}10 on FiQA and ArguAna lifts the baseline. The 4-task nanoBEIR cross-model probe across the three BGE-family models appears in Appendix F.2, Table 16.

The held-out signal also survives at full-BEIR scale. Re-evaluating the default on the full SCIDOCS corpus of 1,000 queries and 25,657 documents with e5-base-v2, SoftCentroid lifts nDCG@10 by +0.54+0.54 at p=0.016p{=}0.016. Stacking light BM25 score fusion (Section 5.6) on top adds a further +0.63+0.63 over pure SoftCentroid at p=0.004p{=}0.004, for a total +1.17+1.17 over the dense baseline at p=0.0001p{=}0.0001. Both the centroid lever and the fusion lever generalize to a held-out task at full-corpus resolution. The lift transfers across embedding-model families on the same held-out SCIDOCS: e5-large-v2 gains +0.77+0.77, gte-base-en-v1.5 gains +0.87+0.87, and bge-large-en-v1.5 gains +0.88+0.88 from SoftCentroid alone with a further +1.54+1.54 from fusion, all at p<0.001p{<}0.001.

A second held-out cell on Touche2020 with a 49-query, 25,000-document subsample preserving all 2,099 gold documents exposes the fusion lever’s compensatory role on a BM25-favorable task. The dense baseline on e5-base-v2 trails BM25 alone, pure SoftCentroid is non-significant, and the fused ranking at w=0.1w{=}0.1 lifts +4.93+4.93 over the dense baseline at p=0.006p{=}0.006 and +6.05+6.05 over pure SoftCentroid at p=0.0001p{=}0.0001. The pattern reproduces across embedding-model families: gte-base-en-v1.5 fusion lifts +5.28+5.28 over baseline, bge-large-en-v1.5 fusion lifts +4.91+4.91, all at p<0.001p{<}0.001, with pure SC non-significant on every model. The full eight-cell held-out matrix is consolidated in Appendix Table 11. NQ and HotpotQA emerge as the next open frontier.

5.5 Comparison with classical Rocchio and PRF baselines

To isolate the contribution of the softmax-weighted centroid over the classical uniform-mean baseline, we compare SoftCentroid against Rocchio at parity.

Classical Rocchio (Rocchio, 1971) is the strongest training-free dense PRF baseline and is mathematically equivalent to the uniform-mean vector PRF of Li et al. (2023a). To position SoftCentroid against this baseline at parity, we grid sixteen classical-Rocchio configurations over K∈{2,3,5,10}K\in\{2,3,5,10\} and β∈{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7}\beta\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\} across all 13 nanoBEIR tasks on both models, then compare SoftCentroid against the best Rocchio per cell.

Decisive positive separation appears on ArguAna across all seven embedding-model families at full-BEIR scale, as Table 4 and Figure 4 report. After a sixteen-cell (K,β)(K,\beta) Rocchio grid, the softmax-weighted SoftCentroid default exceeds the best Rocchio configuration on every model by +2.31+2.31 to +6.00+6.00 nDCG@10, a 1.7×1.7\times to 5.1×5.1\times larger lift, every cell at p<10−4p<10^{-4}. On NFCorpus, SciFact, and FiQA-2018 the two methods land within one nDCG@10 point of each other on e5-base-v2. On nanoBEIR FiQA-2018 with j-v5-nano, SoftCentroid at K=10K{=}10 delivers +1.88+1.88 nDCG@10, exceeding the strongest Rocchio configuration K=10,β=0.7K{=}10,\beta{=}0.7 at +1.34+1.34 by 0.5 nDCG@10. The cells where centroid replacement should help, namely symmetric retrieval, are exactly the cells where SoftCentroid pulls decisively away from the uniform-mean baseline.

Beyond classical Rocchio and sparse PRF, Appendix E compares SoftCentroid against four additional training-free baseline families: alternative centroid-weighting schemes (uniform, linear, cosineγ, hard top-1), Rocchio with explicit negative centroids, iterative multi-pass query refinement, and dimension masking. Across 288 cells spanning three encoder families and four BEIR tasks, no alternative consistently outperforms SoftCentroid. The softmax temperature is the decisive design parameter: uniform and linear weighting trail by 1.01.0–1.11.1 nDCG@10 on average, and Rocchio with negative-centroid subtraction trails by 1.11.1 nDCG@10. Iterative refinement with fresh re-retrieval at each round yields marginal gains on ArguAna (+2.3+2.3 nDCG@10 over SoftCentroid at 2×2\times cost) but regresses on SciFact and FiQA. Dimension masking in the style of ECLIPSE/DIME damages retrieval across all cells, with contrastive subtraction losing 55–77 nDCG@10.

5.6 Sparse-dense score fusion

Sparse pseudo-relevance feedback offers a parallel comparison. We implement RM3 (Lavrenko and Croft, 2001) on full-BEIR NFCorpus and SciFact with a three-cell grid over the standard PRF parameters Kprf∈{5,10}K_{\mathrm{prf}}\in\{5,10\}, |expansion|∈{10,20}|\mathrm{expansion}|\in\{10,20\}, and λorig∈{0.5,0.6}\lambda_{\mathrm{orig}}\in\{0.5,0.6\}. On NFCorpus the best RM3 configuration at Kprf=5K_{\mathrm{prf}}{=}5, 2020 expansion terms, and λ=0.6\lambda{=}0.6 lifts BM25 from 0.2670.267 to 0.2760.276 nDCG@10, a +0.90+0.90 over BM25 that reproduces the standard RM3 direction. BM25+RM3 still trails the dense baseline by 8.008.00 nDCG@10 on NFCorpus and 16.6016.60 on SciFact, both at p<10−4p<10^{-4}. Dense+SoftCentroid on the same embedding model leads BM25+RM3 by 9.119.11 and 17.3517.35 nDCG@10 respectively. The BM25-to-dense gap is 24.024.0 nDCG@10 on FiQA-2018, with BM25 at 0.1590.159 and dense at 0.3990.399. Sparse PRF would have to close this gap to compete, but even an unrealistic perfect-RM3 lift over BM25 cannot bridge it. Sparse PRF inherits the BM25 ceiling. The centroid update operates in the embedding space the model was trained for, while RM3 operates over surface terms.

We further evaluate the strongest learned-sparse PRF baseline SPLADE+RM3, using naver/splade-cocondenser-ensembledistil on a 300-query sample. RM3 lifts SPLADE on NFCorpus by +1.47+1.47 to 0.3630.363 nDCG@10 at p=0.006p{=}0.006 but regresses SPLADE on SciFact by −1.70-1.70 to 0.6850.685 at p=0.04p{=}0.04, because SPLADE’s masked-LM expansion already saturates term-expansion on this task. Dense+SoftCentroid on e5-base-v2, scoring 0.3670.367 on NFCorpus and 0.7220.722 on SciFact, leads the best SPLADE+RM3 configuration on both tasks.

The centroid algebra addresses the dense-retrieval side of the inference recipe; we now ask whether a complementary lexical signal can extend the gains to tasks where pure dense retrieval underperforms.

The geometric ceiling identified in Section 6 bounds what centroid replacement alone can achieve under a frozen single-vector embedding model. A natural orthogonal lever injects a lexical signal alongside the dense ranking. BM25 (Robertson et al., 1995) captures rare-term and exact-match cues that cosine similarity in a learned embedding space can underweight. We adopt score-level fusion rather than the alternative two-stage baseline in which BM25 provides the candidate pool and the dense scorer reranks within it.

The two-stage alternative loses substantial accuracy. On full-BEIR e5-base-v2 NFCorpus, BM25 alone scores 0.2670.267 nDCG@10, a −8.90-8.90-point regression versus the dense baseline at 0.3560.356 at p<10−4p<10^{-4}. The BM25-top-100100-then-dense-rerank pipeline scores 0.3140.314, a −4.18-4.18 regression at p<10−4p<10^{-4}. The same BM25 candidate pool reranked by SoftCentroid scores 0.3150.315, a −4.09-4.09 regression at p<10−4p<10^{-4}. The dense top-KK pool that feeds SoftCentroid’s centroid update is therefore the operative design choice. Routing through a BM25 first stage costs four nDCG@10 points by excluding dense-recoverable relevant documents.

We therefore evaluate SoftCentroid stacked with min-max-normalized BM25 score fusion on all four full-BEIR headline tasks with e5-base-v2, as Table 5 reports. The fused score is (1−w)⋅s~dense+w⋅s~BM25(1{-}w)\cdot\widetilde{s}_{\mathrm{dense}}+w\cdot\widetilde{s}_{\mathrm{BM25}} for a small fusion weight w=0.1w{=}0.1, applied both to the top-KK selection feeding the centroid and to the final ranking.

Fusion lifts the mean lift across the four headline cells from +2.52+2.52 to +3.70+3.70 nDCG@10, and the increment over pure SoftCentroid is statistically significant on three of four cells. The largest gains land where pure SoftCentroid was flat. SciFact gains +2.19+2.19 at p=0.0066p{=}0.0066 and FiQA-2018 gains +1.67+1.67 at p=0.0008p{=}0.0008. Both cells move from p>0.7p{>}0.7 statistical noise under pure SC into the p<0.01p{<}0.01 regime once fusion is added. ArguAna is essentially saturated by pure SoftCentroid, so fusion adds little there. The lexical signal complements the centroid update on tasks where dense retrieval underweights term matches. The centroid update remains the heavier lever on symmetric retrieval where the cosine geometry already favours the document manifold.

The construction transfers across embedding-model families and across a tenfold parameter-scale ladder within the e5 family. Table 6 reports the fusion increment over pure SoftCentroid on five monolithic embedding models. The increment is statistically significant on every cell of the e5 parameter ladder at 33M, 110M, and 335M, with nine of nine cells at p<0.05p{<}0.05, and on at least one cell per model across all five.

The fusion lever generalizes broadly across the 13-task nanoBEIR spectrum. On e5-base-v2, the same default w=0.1w{=}0.1 fusion produces a positive Δ\Delta on 1212 of 1212 retrieval tasks, with mean Δ=+2.93\Delta{=}+2.93 nDCG@10 against −0.22-0.22 for pure SoftCentroid. Pooled across all 599599 nanoBEIR queries, the fusion increment over pure SoftCentroid is +3.14+3.14 nDCG@10 at p<0.0001p{<}0.0001 on a paired bootstrap with 10,00010{,}000 resamples. QA-leaning cells, including HotpotQA, NQ, DBPedia, and Quora, all flip from non-positive under pure SC to positive under fusion, with net gains ranging from +1.61+1.61 on Quora to +5.38+5.38 on HotpotQA. The same construction lifts 1111 of 1212 nanoBEIR tasks on bge-large-en-v1.5 with a mean Δ=+1.88\Delta{=}+1.88 against +0.44+0.44 for pure SoftCentroid, confirming that the breadth of the lift is a property of the fusion construction rather than of e5-base-v2 specifically.

Per-query analysis confirms the lift is broad-based and not driven by outliers. On NFCorpus, the count of queries improved by SC++fusion exceeds the count regressed on every model tested. The net positive margin ranges from +10+10 percentage points on e5-base-v2, where 48%48\% of 247247 evaluable queries improve and 33%33\% regress, to +25+25 percentage points on gte-base-en-v1.5 at 49%49\% improved against 24%24\% regressed.

The fusion lift is also a retrieval-breadth lift, not pure top-ten reranking. On full-BEIR e5-base-v2 NFCorpus, Recall@100 rises from 0.3180.318 at the cosine baseline to 0.3530.353 under pure SoftCentroid, a +3.43+3.43 lift, and to 0.3590.359 under SC++fusion, a +4.06+4.06 lift, both at p<10−4p<10^{-4}. The Recall@100 increment exceeds the nDCG@10 increment, so the lift comes from new relevant documents entering the top hundred rather than reordering inside the top ten. The same pattern holds across embedding-model families. On NFCorpus, the SC++fusion Recall@100 increment exceeds the nDCG@10 increment on e5-small-v2 at +2.62+2.62 against +1.82+1.82, on e5-base-v2 at +4.06+4.06 against +1.79+1.79, on e5-large-v2 at +3.93+3.93 against +2.51+2.51, and on gte-base-en-v1.5 at +2.77+2.77 against +2.20+2.20, all at p<10−3p<10^{-3} for the Recall@100 lift. SciFact already saturates Recall@100 at 0.960.96 under cosine. FiQA-2018 follows NFCorpus directionally on nDCG@10 with a +1.73+1.73 lift, and the same Recall@100 versus nDCG@10 pattern on FiQA-2018 reproduces on e5-small-v2 at +2.03+2.03 against +1.38+1.38 and e5-large-v2 at +2.12+2.12 against +1.29+1.29, both at p<0.05p<0.05.

The chosen weight w=0.1w{=}0.1 sits inside a wide stable region rather than at a knife edge, both within and across embedding-model families. On full-BEIR e5-base-v2 NFCorpus the lift ranges from +1.32+1.32 at w=0.05w{=}0.05 to +1.97+1.97 at w=0.15w{=}0.15 before fading to +1.15+1.15 at w=0.25w{=}0.25, with the four values w≤0.20w\leq 0.20 all statistically significant at p<0.01p<0.01 on the paired bootstrap. The same sweep on three additional models e5-large-v2, bge-large-en-v1.5, and gte-base-en-v1.5 reproduces the pattern. Every model peaks within w∈[0.05,0.15]w\in[0.05,0.15] and the paper-default w=0.10w{=}0.10 is significant at p<0.01p<0.01 on every cell of all four models, with Δ\Delta ranging from +1.39+1.39 on bge-large-en-v1.5 to +2.51+2.51 on e5-large-v2. Only w=0.25w{=}0.25 drops to non-significance. The default w=0.10w{=}0.10 used throughout the cross-model and 13-task experiments is therefore a conservative point inside a 4×4{\times}-wide robust region that is itself robust across embedding-model families. The ww sweep was conducted at the default K=3K{=}3; the KK sweep in Appendix D was conducted without BM25 fusion. The two parameters are geometrically orthogonal: KK controls how many documents contribute to the centroid while ww controls the fraction of lexical signal injected into the final score. In practice, varying KK within its stable region {2,3}\{2,3\} while holding w=0.10w{=}0.10 fixed produces lift changes of at most 0.30.3 nDCG@10, confirming that the two levers can be set independently.

5.7 Frontier by substrate family

The centroid families dominate every other substrate when programs are grouped by family on j-v5-small. The Rocchio, SoftCentroid, and FirstSent centroid families are the consistent winners on the three retrieval-style tasks. Three other substrate families do not contribute to the frontier on j-v5-small: LoRAFusion stays close to baseline, DropoutEns adds no signal, and AsymLoRA consistently underperforms. A targeted document-projection probe that replaces each document’s embedding with the projection of its first-paragraph centroid sits at −1.11-1.11 on DBPedia, indicating that doc-side projection alone is insufficient without a coupled query-side update. Table 7 reports the per-family and per-task breakdown.

5.8 Regimes of test-time compute

The experimental evidence across seven embedding-model families, thirteen retrieval tasks, and two held-out benchmarks converges on a unified geometric picture.

The cosine paradigm is not erased by test-time compute, only wrapped. Three regimes emerge from the discovered frontier: the paradigm breaks on symmetric retrieval, bends on medical-IR headlines, and holds on QA-leaning asymmetric tasks. Figure 5 summarizes this taxonomy across the four headline tasks and the two embedding-model families.

The paradigm breaks on symmetric retrieval. On ArguAna, frontier programs gain six to seven nDCG@10 points over the cosine baseline on j-v5-small and j-v5-nano, with 99% retention under dev/test validation. On a second embedding-model family, the same default SoftCentroid gains over ten points on full-BEIR e5-base-v2 at p<0.0001p<0.0001, as Table 3 reports. This is large enough to call the trivial program P0P_{0} dominated on symmetric retrieval across both embedding-model families. The break is enabled by the symmetry of the task: query and document are drawn from the same distribution, which makes “move 𝐪\mathbf{q} onto the document manifold” the right operation. The cosine geometry is not abandoned. The program exploits it more aggressively than P0P_{0} does.

The paradigm bends on medical-IR headlines. On NFCorpus, the default SoftCentroid program gains +2.0+2.0 to +2.4+2.4 nDCG@10 with p<0.001p<0.001, and 67 to 80% of the oracle gain survives validation. The lift is real but bounded. It is large enough to be worth the two extra matrix multiplies and small enough that one cannot say cosine plus single-forward is dominated. The geometry is the same, used with a slightly larger program.

The paradigm holds on QA-leaning asymmetric tasks for the centroid algebra alone, but the fusion lever from Section 5.6 closes much of the gap. Pure SoftCentroid on NQ and HotpotQA produces at most a neutral effect, with full-BEIR e5-base-v2 NQ yielding a small positive lift under K=3K{=}3. The structural reason is that the local top-KK document centroid is dominated by lexical-overlap neighbours of the question. “What answers this question” is harder to estimate from the document manifold alone. Composing SoftCentroid with light BM25 score fusion moves these cells decisively. On e5-base-v2 13-task nanoBEIR, NQ flips from −0.06-0.06 under pure SC to +0.93+0.93 under SC++fusion, a net +0.99+0.99, and HotpotQA flips from −2.58-2.58 to +2.80+2.80, a net +5.38+5.38. The QA limitation of pure centroid replacement is thus an addressable boundary rather than a fundamental ceiling, with sparse-dense fusion as the productive direction. Lifting it further would call for an external generator or a task-specific adapter, both outside the training-free, LLM-free regime studied here.

6 Discussion

Our contribution is not that centroid replacement helps, which is consistent with classical PRF, but the positive separation between document-manifold programs and stochastic ensembling. Among the seventeen substrate families explored, document-manifold programs form a distinct frontier dominating stochastic ensembling on every cell where they fire, with 99% of oracle gain retained on ArguAna under dev/test selection. ArguAna retrieves counter-arguments where query and document are drawn from the same distribution. Replacing 𝐪\mathbf{q} with the weighted mean of the top documents moves it onto the document manifold, exactly the right place under symmetric retrieval. The K=1K{=}1 setting that replaces the query with the top-1 document alone gives +6.4+6.4 to +7.1+7.1 on ArguAna while losing 3 to 4 points on asymmetric SciFact and FiQA.

The agentic loop’s contribution is not the algebraic recipe, which is close to known PRF, but the autoresearch artifact. The default K=3,α=0.5,τ=0.05K{=}3,\alpha{=}0.5,\tau{=}0.05 ports across seven embedding-model families without a per-task hyperparameter sweep, and the lesson ledger documents which substrate families do not generalize. Rocchio remains a strong simple baseline. What the generation loop adds is the absence of grid-search overhead and a reusable scaffolding for re-running the search on any embedding model. The parameter sensitivity of this default is visualized in Figure 10 in Appendix D, which shows per-task lift across the α\alpha, KK, and τ\tau sweeps on e5-base-v2.

Practical deployment relies on approximate nearest-neighbour search rather than exact cosine. We measure the lift’s robustness to HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2020) parameter variation on e5-base-v2 NFCorpus with two ANN calls per query, one for the initial top-KK pool used to construct the centroid and one for the rescoring of the updated query 𝐪′\mathbf{q}^{\prime}. The lift is invariant across efSearch ∈{16,32,64,128,256}\in\{16,32,64,128,256\} with Δ∈[+1.45,+1.53]\Delta\in[+1.45,+1.53], efConstruction ∈{40,100,200,400}\in\{40,100,200,400\} with Δ∈[+1.44,+1.63]\Delta\in[+1.44,+1.63], and graph degree M∈{8,16,32,64}M\in\{8,16,32,64\} with Δ∈[+1.46,+1.56]\Delta\in[+1.46,+1.56]. Every cell is significant at p<0.01p<0.01 on the paired bootstrap. Centroid replacement therefore composes with off-the-shelf ANN stacks without parameter-specific tuning.

End-to-end latency on the same NFCorpus index measures 12.5312.53 ms baseline and 13.2713.27 ms with SoftCentroid on an NVIDIA L4 GPU, a +0.75+0.75 ms or +6%+6\% overhead. The corresponding CPU numbers are 48.4148.41 ms and 49.4949.49 ms, a +1.08+1.08 ms or +2%+2\% overhead. The encoder forward pass dominates wall-clock in both regimes, and the second HNSW call plus centroid construction add sub-millisecond overhead.

The pattern across the three regimes is that direct ports of the LLM TTC playbook diverge from the discovered frontier. DropoutEns, the best-of-NN analogue, sits at baseline. AsymLoRA, which samples under different LoRA conditioning, sits well below baseline because asymmetric LoRA misaligns the query and document subspaces. Generative TTC wins because the output space is discrete and a verifier collapses a noisy distribution to a sharper mode. A dense embedding model’s output is a single point on the unit sphere 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}. Averaging MM stochastic embeddings leaves 𝕊d−1\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, and re-normalizing projects onto a Karcher-mean approximation in a metric the embedding model was not trained to respect. There is also no inference-time verifier signal. What works is operations that respect the ranking algebra. Rocchio-style updates keep 𝐪\mathbf{q} near its trained location and nudge it toward the local centroid the embedding model already considers similar.

Every frontier program leaves the cosine geometry intact and uses extra inference compute to find a better point in it. This is the empirical ceiling under a frozen single-vector embedding model with no second model and no extra training. Lifting it will require either changing the embedding model, through multi-vector late interaction or trained TTC adapters, or admitting an external generator in the inference path.

The value of the agentic loop relative to a focused grid search over centroid variants deserves explicit discussion. A researcher who already knows that Rocchio-style updates are the right direction can define a grid over (K,α,τ,anchor)(K,\alpha,\tau,\text{anchor}) and recover SoftCentroid in a few hundred evaluations. The loop adds value on three axes that a focused grid cannot. First, the loop explores substrate families the researcher may not anticipate: 259 programs span 17 substrate families, and approximately 170 of those programs are anti-patterns, specifically LoRA fusion, dropout ensembles, dimension gating, and score-space-only methods, whose falsification is itself informative. The lesson ledger accumulates these ruled-out hypotheses so any future search on a new embedding model can skip structurally equivalent ideas without re-running them. Second, convergence to the centroid family was an emergent finding rather than a preset hypothesis. The loop started with LLM-TTC substrates and discovered centroid replacement after those failed. A focused centroid grid assumes the conclusion. Third, the lesson ledger is a reusable artifact: dropping in a different embedding model means the proposer skips the 170 known anti-patterns immediately, concentrating evaluations on the open hypotheses.

That said, if a researcher already knows that pseudo-relevance feedback in embedding space is the productive direction, a focused centroid grid will converge faster than the unsupervised loop. The loop’s comparative advantage is hypothesis generation under uncertainty, not parameter optimization once the winning substrate family is known.

The universality criterion’s gating set, defined as {NFCorpus, SciFact, ArguAna}, affects which programs are admitted to the frontier. We assess this sensitivity post-hoc using the e5-base-v2 13-task nanoBEIR evaluation from Section F. Replacing the gating set with {NFCorpus, FiQA-2018, SciFact} still admits SoftCentroid as universal positive (per-task deltas +0.58+0.58, +1.66+1.66, +0.55+0.55). Replacing it with {NQ, HotpotQA, ArguAna} excludes SoftCentroid because NQ (−0.42-0.42) and HotpotQA (−1.31-1.31) are negative under pure centroid replacement; those cells are recovered by the BM25 fusion lever described in Section 5.6. Using all 13 tasks as a strict gating criterion also excludes SoftCentroid (8 of 13 positive). The original gating set therefore represents a conservative but achievable coverage criterion that spans medical IR, scientific fact verification, and symmetric retrieval, the three paradigms where pure centroid algebra produces reliable lift. QA-leaning gating sets would have directed the search toward hybrid programs earlier, but such programs were not fully within the training-free, no-LLM substrate constraint.

The anchor choice for the 2×2\times regime was explored beyond FirstSent. Generation 89 of the search tested two title-field variants at 2×2\times cost: P256 (title-only encoding as a robustness witness gate) and P257 (title as the interpolation anchor, replacing the first sentence). Both programs produce positive lift on ArguAna across both j-v5 model sizes (P256: +3.78+3.78 small, +4.54+4.54 nano; P257: +5.20+5.20 small, +5.26+5.26 nano), and P257 delivers the second-largest 2×2\times ArguAna gain after FirstSent. However, neither achieves universal-positive status: both programs remain MARGINAL on NFCorpus for j-v5-small, with gains of +0.47+0.47 and +0.40+0.40 respectively that fall below the p<0.05p<0.05 significance threshold. The lesson ledger records this as the structural reason: the curated title field carries the argument topic on ArguAna debate corpora but does not reliably signal medical-document relevance on NFCorpus, where the first sentence of the body carries the clinical framing that the title does not. FirstSent avoids this task-specificity by extracting the opening of the body rather than the metadata field. Alternative anchors such as last sentence or mid-document argmax sentence were also tested and either regressed on ArguAna or remained MARGINAL. Full investigation of anchor selection strategies is left to future work.

7 Conclusion

The common reading that test-time compute is reserved for large reasoning LLMs does not hold for the class of embedding models distilled from those same LLMs. A frozen single-vector embedding model admits a structured, model-family-agnostic class of test-time interventions whose discovery is the contribution of this paper. The boundary the search exposes is geometric rather than empirical. Stochastic best-of-NN aggregators leave the unit sphere and lose the ranking algebra. Structured updates that move the query toward the local document centroid survive across seven embedding-model families at full-BEIR scale, with statistically significant gains on the symmetric and medical-IR headlines and held-out lifts on SCIDOCS and Touche2020. A complementary BM25 score fusion lever stacked on top of SoftCentroid broadens the gain across the wider nanoBEIR suite.

The most useful artefact is not the winning program but the rerunnable loop, lesson ledger, and program registry that produced it. Drop in a different embedding-model family or benchmark and the same loop will produce a different frontier subject to the same geometric ceiling. The cosine paradigm is not erased by test-time compute, only wrapped. The remaining open question is whether that ceiling can be lifted from inside the cosine paradigm, or only by changing the embedding model.

Appendix A Baseline Reproduction

Appendix B Cost-Accuracy Pareto Frontier and Test-Time Scaling

Figure 6 shows the per-cell Pareto frontiers for all 259 registered programs.

Figure 7 plots the mean Δ\Delta nDCG@10 of every program in the registry against its test-time cost factor cc, with the Pareto upper envelope marked in red. Table 9 aggregates the same 1,522 program-task evaluations. At each cost stratum it reports the best mean Δ\Delta nDCG@10, averaged across the four BEIR tasks, any program achieved. The frontier saturates between 2×2\times and 4×4\times: doubling encoder forward-pass cost beyond 2×2\times buys at most +0.05+0.05 mean nDCG@10. Above 4×4\times, no program in the registry improves on the 4×4\times champion, and several high-cost programs at ≥50×\geq 50\times regress sharply when their multi-LoRA gates produce misaligned anchors. The empirical scaling is qualitatively distinct from the log-linear best-of-NN curve reported for generative TTC (Brown et al., 2024). Dense-retrieval test-time compute is concave and bounded by the geometric ceiling of the cosine paradigm.

A complementary form of test-time scaling, internal to the centroid algebra itself, is to iterate SoftCentroid multiple times on the same encoded query. On full-BEIR ArguAna, where the dense baseline is far from the document manifold, iterating the centroid update lifts the result further on every model tested, as Table 10 reports. The single-iteration default already yields lifts ranging from +3.56+3.56 on gte-base-en-v1.5 to +12.55+12.55 on e5-base-v2 at p<10−4p<10^{-4}. Iterating to the model-specific peak between iters two and five adds a further +0.91+0.91 to +3.18+3.18 nDCG@10 at p<10−4p<10^{-4} on all seven models. Extending the grid on e5-base-v2 to twenty iterations confirms a clear peak rather than unbounded growth, as Figure 8 shows. The lift saturates at +15.73+15.73 at iter 55, decays gently to +15.26+15.26, +14.74+14.74, +14.22+14.22, and +14.01+14.01 at iters 7,10,15,207,10,15,20, and remains statistically significant at p<10−4p<10^{-4} throughout.

ArguAna therefore admits deeper test-time scaling within the discovered algebraic family across the entire embedding-model family, not just one. We retain the single-iteration default in the main results because the universality criterion of Section 3 requires non-negativity across the full task spectrum, and iteration-budget transfer is itself task-dependent. The pattern reproduces on held-out SCIDOCS at full-BEIR scale with e5-base-v2. Iter 11 peaks at +0.54+0.54 at p=0.016p{=}0.016 and the lift decays through iters 22, 33, 44, 55 to +0.46+0.46 ns, +0.21+0.21, +0.12+0.12, +0.10+0.10. This confirms that the iteration axis is not held-out-restricted but rather task-restricted, with single-step updates serving as the safe default outside ArguAna-like manifolds.

The two paper-level levers compose orthogonally. Stacking BM25 fusion from Section 5.6 on iterative SoftCentroid for e5-base-v2 elevates the iteration trajectory across all three medical-IR and finance-IR headlines tested. On NFCorpus, fusion lifts the iter-one, two, and three deltas from +1.11+1.11, +0.41+0.41, −0.06-0.06 under pure SC to +1.79+1.79, +1.60+1.60, +1.62+1.62, with p≤0.015p\leq 0.015 on every fused cell. Pure SC on the same model loses significance after iter one. The same fusion lever moves SciFact’s three deltas from +0.25+0.25, −0.49-0.49, −1.46-1.46 to +1.10+1.10, +0.41+0.41, −0.32-0.32, and FiQA-2018’s from +0.01+0.01, −1.07-1.07, −1.54-1.54 to +1.73+1.73 at p=0.004p{=}0.004, then +0.73+0.73, then −0.17-0.17. The lexical signal therefore stabilizes the centroid update across iterations rather than adding a constant offset. On the three tasks tested, every iter-one fused cell either stays in or moves into positive territory.

The same stabilization holds across embedding-model families. On NFCorpus, fusion lifts the iter-one through iter-three trajectory into statistical significance at p<0.05p<0.05 on every cell of e5-small-v2, e5-base-v2, e5-large-v2, and gte-base-en-v1.5, with deltas ranging from +1.39+1.39 to +2.60+2.60 at iter two when pure SC on the same models has already lost significance on three of four. The two task-LoRA j-v5-small and j-v5-nano headline models show the same pattern. Fusion holds iter three at +1.66∗+1.66^{\ast}{} on j-v5-small where pure SC sits at +0.96+0.96 ns, and elevates iter two to +1.86∗+1.86^{\ast}{} on j-v5-nano where pure SC sits at +1.21+1.21 ns. A controlled iteration-budget schedule that tightens the centroid pull when the local manifold is symmetric and freezes after one step otherwise is a productive direction for future work, but lies outside the program family explored by the present search.

Appendix C Held-Out Cross-Model Validation

Table 11 consolidates the held-out full-BEIR evidence reported inline in Section 5, and Figure 9 visualises the eight cells. SCIDOCS uses 1,000 queries and a 25,657-document corpus with multi-relevance labels, averaging around 30 gold documents per query. Touche2020 uses 49 queries on a 25,000-document subsample that preserves all 2,099 gold documents in a BM25-favorable argumentation domain. Both tasks were strictly held out from the agentic loop’s frontier-admission gate. The table reports paired-bootstrap Δ\Delta nDCG@10 with 10,00010{,}000 resamples on per-query nDCG@10. Appendix D SoftCentroid Hyperparameter Ablation

Table 13 reports the one-parameter ablation around the recommended default K=3,α=0.5,τ=0.05K{=}3,\alpha{=}0.5,\tau{=}0.05 on j-v5-small and j-v5-nano. Interpolation α\alpha and softmax temperature τ\tau carry most of the gain. Centroid size KK is largely inert across K∈{3,5,8}K\in\{3,5,8\}. On e5-base-v2, the same one-parameter sweep at full-BEIR scale reproduces the j-v5 pattern and surfaces the same task-specific asymmetry seen for iterative SoftCentroid in Section B. NFCorpus has a clear stable region around the default, with α∈[0.2,0.5]\alpha\in[0.2,0.5] at p<0.01p<0.01, τ∈{0.02,0.05}\tau\in\{0.02,0.05\} at p≤0.02p\leq 0.02, and K∈{2,3}K\in\{2,3\} at p<0.01p<0.01. ArguAna scales monotonically along every axis.

Figure 10 visualizes the full α\alpha, KK, and τ\tau sweeps on e5-base-v2 as heat maps. Each cell encodes Δ\Delta nDCG@10 (×100\times 100) versus the cosine baseline, with the paper default (bold border) sitting in a clear positive region on NFCorpus and exhibiting monotonic improvement on ArguAna. The FiQA-2018 and SciFact panels confirm that most parameter choices produce near-zero or slightly positive delta on those tasks; the slight negative values at large KK and large τ\tau on SciFact are not statistically significant. The visualization makes the task-asymmetry story immediate: any α≥0.2\alpha\geq 0.2, any K≤5K\leq 5, and any τ≤0.05\tau\leq 0.05 sustains the NFCorpus lift, while ArguAna rewards pushing every parameter toward its extreme.

The ArguAna monotonicity replicates across the full seven-model cohort on every aggressive direction, namely smaller τ\tau, larger α\alpha, and smaller KK, as Table 12 reports. Combined with the iterative-SC peak at iter five from Section B, ArguAna admits deeper test-time intervention on four independent axes across embedding-model families, with 7777 of 7777 aggressive-direction cells significant at p<10−4p<10^{-4}. Every model gains by sharpening the centroid through smaller τ\tau and smaller KK, and by giving more weight to the centroid in the interpolation through larger α\alpha. This is consistent with the symmetric-retrieval geometry in which the document and query manifolds coincide. The universal default is the conservative pick that survives the cross-task universality criterion of Section 3. The asymmetric admission of more aggressive parameters on ArguAna is the same geometric story.

Appendix E Extended Baseline Comparisons

Table 14 compares SoftCentroid against four families of training-free alternatives under the same frozen-encoder regime. All methods use K=3K{=}3 and α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 to match the SoftCentroid default. Mean Δ\Delta nDCG@10 (×100\times 100) is averaged across three encoder families (e5-base-v2, j-v5-small, bge-large-en-v1.5).

The hard top-1 variant (replacing the query with the single nearest document embedding) deserves comment: it is the α=1.0,K=1\alpha{=}1.0,K{=}1 limit of SoftCentroid and was independently discovered by the agentic loop as the PseudoDoc substrate in early generations (see Section 4). Its strong ArguAna result exploits the symmetric argument-counterargument structure of that task, while the regressions on SciFact and FiQA confirm the task-specificity documented in the lesson ledger. The SoftCentroid default at K=3K{=}3 with softmax weighting represents the robust middle ground that generalizes across tasks.

Appendix F Cross-Model Transfer Details

F.1 13-Task nanoBEIR Transfer

The model-specificity pattern observed at the headline scale also appears across the broader 13-task nanoBEIR suite. Table 15 applies three frontier SoftCentroid variants from the j-v5 search to e5-base-v2 across all 13 nanoBEIR retrieval tasks at the 50-query sub-sample. The K=10K{=}10 variant emerges as the strongest default on this monolithic embedding model.

F.2 4-Task nanoBEIR Probe

Table 16 compares three SoftCentroid variants on three monolithic embedding models e5-base-v2, bge-base-en-v1.5, and bge-small-en-v1.5 across the four headline BEIR tasks at the 50-query nanoBEIR slice. e5-base-v2 surfaces as the strongest of the three and was selected for the full-BEIR validation in Table 3.

Appendix G Program Flowcharts

Sixteen representative embedding programs from the agent’s registry are rendered as flow diagrams. Each diagram shows the sequence of encode, retrieve, aggregate, interpolate, and rerank operations the program executes at inference. The programs span the centroid, anchor, gating, and multi-LoRA substrates explored over ninety generations. Collectively they trace the convergence of the discovered algebra.

Appendix H Limitations and Scope

The proposer is itself an LLM agent and inherits whatever priors the underlying model encodes about which substrates are worth exploring. The explicit lesson ledger and the dev/test paired-bootstrap protocol partially mitigate this, but proposer bias cannot be eliminated. A different proposer could traverse the embedding-program space differently. The generation loop is a heuristic search and offers no coverage or optimality guarantee. The lesson ledger reduces redundant exploration but does not certify that the discovered frontier is globally optimal.

Headline experiments use j-v5-small and j-v5-nano. Full-BEIR cross-model validation extends to e5-small-v2, e5-base-v2, e5-large-v2, gte-base-en-v1.5, and bge-large-en-v1.5 for the fusion lever, as Table 6 shows. For iterative SoftCentroid on ArguAna and the Rocchio comparison, the same five models together with j-v5-small and j-v5-nano make up the seven-model cohort summarized in Tables 10 and 4. The optimal cluster size KK is model-specific. bge-base-en-v1.5 is partial and bge-small-en-v1.5 marks the parameter-scale boundary. The algebra is most reliable on models at or above one hundred million parameters. The multi-LoRA adapter design of j-v5 also enables substrate families such as LoRAFusion and AsymLoRA that do not apply to monolithic embedding models, so those specific anti-patterns may not generalize. We evaluate on English BEIR. Performance on multilingual, conversational, or code-retrieval benchmarks is unknown.

The 50-query nanoBEIR slices carry sub-sample variance; we recommend full-BEIR validation before deploying any specific configuration.

Future work can extend the registry by integrating LLM-assisted methods such as HyDE (Gao et al., 2023), LLM-VPRF (Li et al., 2025b), and GPRF (Tu et al., 2026), alongside trained dense-PRF such as ANCE-PRF (Yu et al., 2021), as separate proposers in the loop; each occupies a different inference regime than the training-free, no-LLM substrate explored here.
